interview_metadata.name: Kyle Joffrion
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I grew up around the Boston suburbs in a pretty middle-class New England family. My parents were the kind of people who cared a lot about school, but they also let me chase weird interests. As a kid I was always taking apart old electronics, drawing robots in notebooks, and making little games on the family computer. Sports were around too because my family is very Boston sports oriented, so Celtics games and Red Sox games were kind of background noise in the house. In high school I got serious about coding and art at the same time. I was not the most organized person, honestly, but I could disappear for a whole weekend making a little interactive animation or wiring LEDs to a sensor. I finished school on an accelerated path and completed a bachelor's in Computer Science with a Visual Arts minor. College was where I found my people: hackathon friends, artists, improv people, and the kind of classmates who would argue about code structure at 2 a.m. over iced coffee. I am 18 now, never married, no kids, living in Boston near the Fenway/Kenmore area, and I am not working a regular job at the moment. I am trying to line up an internship or entry-level creative technology role. A major thing for me has been realizing that I do not want to choose between being technical and being creative. I want to build interactive installations, public art, maybe immersive data-driven spaces, and eventually start something of my own.

follow_ups.question: What was your family like day to day when you were growing up?
follow_ups.response: Pretty normal and busy. My mom kept the house organized, my dad was more of the practical fix-it person, and dinner was usually the time everyone checked in. We did Thanksgiving, Fourth of July, and a lot of Boston sports watching.

follow_ups.question: When did coding and art first really connect for you?
follow_ups.response: Probably around sophomore year of high school. I made this glitchy browser animation for an art class, and people actually reacted to it like it was art, not just a nerd project.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was choosing whether to focus only on computer science or keep visual art as a serious part of my life. There was a point where I thought the practical thing was to just grind LeetCode, get a software job, and keep art as a hobby. Then I joined a hackathon team that built an interactive projection piece using motion sensors and JavaScript visuals. It was chaotic; we barely slept and the wiring kept failing. But when people walked up and started moving around with the piece, I felt like, okay, this is the lane. I changed how I picked classes after that, added more visual arts work, did more 3D modeling, and started looking at human-computer interaction. It made me feel less like I had two separate identities.

follow_ups.question: Who was involved in that hackathon project?
follow_ups.response: My friends Maya, Theo, and Priya were on that team. Maya is more design-focused, Theo is a C++ and hardware person, and Priya is great at keeping everyone from drifting too far off task.

follow_ups.question: What did your parents think about that choice?
follow_ups.response: They were supportive but a little nervous. They understood computer science, but interactive art sounded less stable to them until I explained there are real jobs around creative technology and HCI.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was both. The first spark just happened because the project felt right, but after that I made a pretty conscious decision to stop treating art like a side quest.

follow_ups.question: What did that decision change in practical terms?
follow_ups.response: I chose classes and projects that mixed design, code, and user experience instead of only systems or algorithms.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever second-guess it?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, especially when friends were chasing more straightforward software internships. I still worry about money, but the creative-tech route feels more like me.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: A mentor would have helped a lot. I had professors and friends, but someone already working in creative technology could have made the path feel less blurry.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Just seeing examples of portfolios, internships, and job titles. The field can feel invisible unless you already know the language.

follow_ups.question: Are you seeking that kind of help now?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I have been going to maker space events and asking older students and local artists how they got started.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner or children. I have never been married. My parents are still really important to me, even though I live more independently now. My mom is the person I call when I am spiraling about logistics or money because she is very practical. My dad is more the person I talk to about building things, cars, circuits, and sports. I also have a younger sister, Lily, who is still in high school, and we send each other dumb videos and sometimes talk about music. My family is close but not super intense. We usually see each other every couple weeks if I go back to the suburbs, and holidays are a big deal. I think being near Boston helps because I can have my own life but still get home pretty easily.

follow_ups.question: How often do you talk with your parents?
follow_ups.response: My mom texts me a few times a week, and I usually call home on Sundays or when something practical comes up.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your sister do together?
follow_ups.response: When I am home, we might get coffee, watch a Celtics game, or I help her with computer stuff for school.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: No one else immediate besides my parents and my sister. I have grandparents and cousins around Massachusetts, but day to day it is mainly my parents and Lily.

follow_ups.question: Do you see extended family often?
follow_ups.response: Mostly holidays and summer cookouts.

follow_ups.question: Are you close with any cousins?
follow_ups.response: I have one cousin in Cambridge I text about concerts sometimes, but we are not daily-close.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My friends are a huge part of my life. Maya, Theo, Priya, and Jordan are probably my core group right now. We do hackathons, grab cheap food, go to shows, and sometimes play pickup basketball on weekends. I also have improv friends from Improv Asylum classes and open nights. I am not in a serious romantic relationship. I have dated a little, but honestly my life is pretty project-heavy and messy right now.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your closest friends?
follow_ups.response: Usually several times a week, even if it is just working in the same room or getting late-night food.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually do together?
follow_ups.response: Code, sketch, play basketball, go mural-hunting, cook badly, or end up at a concert if someone found cheap tickets.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Boston, around the Fenway/Kenmore side of things, zip code 02215. It is very student-heavy, with a lot of apartments, coffee shops, music venues, and people constantly moving through. I like that I can walk or take the T almost anywhere useful. There is street art, random galleries, cheap-ish food if you know where to look, and the Charles River is close enough for jogging when I am actually being responsible. It can be loud, and rent is ridiculous, but creatively it feels alive.

follow_ups.question: Where do you spend the most time nearby?
follow_ups.response: Coffee shops, campus-adjacent maker spaces, the river path, and friends' apartments.

follow_ups.question: What do you like least about the area?
follow_ups.response: Rent, noise, and how crowded the sidewalks and trains get around games or concerts.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I mostly feel safe. I pay attention late at night, especially walking back from shows or hackathons, but I do not feel scared living here.

follow_ups.question: Are there places you avoid?
follow_ups.response: Not really, but I avoid empty side streets after midnight if I am alone.

follow_ups.question: Do your friends feel similarly?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, though my female friends are more careful about walking alone, which makes sense.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is access: art, transit, friends, food, music, classes, everything. The downside is cost and how little quiet there is.

follow_ups.question: Does the neighborhood affect your routine?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. Because everything is close, I say yes to more events than I probably should.

follow_ups.question: Would you stay there long term?
follow_ups.response: Maybe for a while, but long term I would want somewhere cheaper with studio or workshop space.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live with two roommates, Jordan and Sam, in a rented apartment. Jordan is also into design and music, and Sam is more pre-med and very schedule-based, which balances the apartment out. We each have our own room and share the kitchen and living room. It is not fancy, but it works. There are cables, sketchbooks, and takeout containers around more often than Sam would prefer.

follow_ups.question: How do household chores work?
follow_ups.response: We have a loose rotation, but Sam is the only one who actually remembers it, so he reminds us.

follow_ups.question: Do you eat meals together?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a week. Kimchi fried rice nights happen when I get ambitious.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone living there now is a regular household member on the lease.

follow_ups.question: Any short-term sublets right now?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any plans for someone to move soon?
follow_ups.response: Not immediately.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Friends crash on the couch sometimes after late shows or hackathons, but nobody regularly lives there.

follow_ups.question: Who most often stays over?
follow_ups.response: Usually Theo or Maya if the T is inconvenient late at night.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone who lives here is currently here.

follow_ups.question: Any roommates away for the summer?
follow_ups.response: Not yet.

follow_ups.question: Anyone away for health reasons?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week is kind of uneven. On weekdays I usually wake up around 8:30 or 9 if I do not have anything early, make coffee, check messages, and work on portfolio projects or internship applications. Afternoons might be coding, sketching, meeting friends, or going to a maker space. Evenings are unpredictable: improv, a show, pickup basketball, or just working late on some idea. Weekends are more social. I might play basketball, wander around photographing murals, go to a gallery, or take a quick trip with friends.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Too late, honestly. Midnight is good for me; 2 a.m. happens if I am coding.

follow_ups.question: What is the most regular part of your week?
follow_ups.response: Coffee in the morning and checking GitHub or messages before I do anything serious.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: Right now I am not working a paid job. I just finished my bachelor's, and I am in that awkward zone of applying for internships and entry-level creative tech roles. I do unpaid portfolio work, hackathon organizing, and occasional volunteer-type maker space stuff, but nothing with a paycheck at the moment. My 'work' hours are self-imposed, usually late morning through afternoon, but I am not great at keeping it cleanly separated from nights.

follow_ups.question: What kinds of roles are you applying for?
follow_ups.response: Creative technologist, junior front-end developer, HCI research assistant, interactive media intern, that kind of thing.

follow_ups.question: How many applications have you sent lately?
follow_ups.response: Maybe fifteen in the last month, plus a bunch of informal messages to people.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I try to keep up with apartment chores, family check-ins, and helping friends with projects. I also maintain a few code repos and update my portfolio site. I volunteer occasionally at maker space events, usually helping set up hardware or showing younger students how to prototype basic interactive stuff. It is not formal every week, but I try to show up when I said I would.

follow_ups.question: What chores are yours?
follow_ups.response: Trash, recycling, and cleaning the kitchen counters, though I am not perfect at it.

follow_ups.question: What maker space work do you do?
follow_ups.response: Mostly setup, troubleshooting Arduino-style circuits, and helping beginners connect code to physical inputs.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The big change is finishing school and not having classes structure my day. It is nice because I have more freedom, but it is also weird because I have to create my own schedule. I have been trying to treat job searching like a job, but some days I drift into a project for six hours and forget practical stuff. I am also jogging a little more now that the weather is better.

follow_ups.question: What do you miss about school structure?
follow_ups.response: Deadlines and seeing people automatically. Without that, I have to manufacture momentum.

follow_ups.question: What new habit has helped most?
follow_ups.response: Writing three tasks on a sticky note in the morning. Not a full planner, just three things.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so that does not apply to me.

follow_ups.question: Do you help care for any younger relatives?
follow_ups.response: Not regularly. I help my sister with school tech stuff sometimes.

follow_ups.question: Do child care responsibilities affect your schedule?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not had major direct experiences with law enforcement. Mostly it is seeing police around games, concerts, protests, or on the T. I have been stopped once with friends late at night near a closed campus building because someone thought we looked suspicious carrying equipment, but it ended quickly when we explained we were coming from a project setup.

follow_ups.question: How did that stop feel?
follow_ups.response: Mostly awkward and tense. I was aware it probably went smoother for me than it might for someone else.

follow_ups.question: Did it change your behavior?
follow_ups.response: A little. I keep project gear in bags now instead of walking around with wires and tripods visible.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Seeing police presence at protests and around big sports events stands out. It can feel like crowd control more than community safety.

follow_ups.question: Have you attended protests?
follow_ups.response: I have been to a couple local demonstrations, mostly with friends.

follow_ups.question: Did anything happen there involving police?
follow_ups.response: Nothing dramatic to me personally, but the line of officers changed the mood.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and no close family member has been arrested as far as I know. I know acquaintances who have had minor trouble, but not close friends.

follow_ups.question: Any court involvement in your close circle?
follow_ups.response: No, not in my immediate circle.

follow_ups.question: Does arrest come up as a worry for you?
follow_ups.response: Not personally, but I think about it politically and socially.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I am newly eligible, so I do not have a long voting history. I plan to vote, especially in national and Massachusetts elections, but I am still learning the local ballot stuff. I pay attention more than some of my friends, but I am not someone who has voted in every election yet because I only recently turned 18.

follow_ups.question: Have you registered to vote?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in Massachusetts.

follow_ups.question: What elections feel most important to you?
follow_ups.response: President, Senate, governor, and local issues around housing and transit.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as left-leaning or progressive, but not extremely ideological in a party-machine way. I care a lot about climate, housing costs, public transit, racial justice, LGBTQ rights, and funding education. Being in Boston, you see how much opportunity there is but also how expensive and unequal it can be. I am skeptical of big corporations when they act like innovation solves everything while people cannot afford rent. At the same time, I like technology and startups, so I am not anti-business. I just think public goods matter and people need a fair shot. I am closest to Democrats, but I do not think any party is magically clean or perfect.

follow_ups.question: Where did those views come from?
follow_ups.response: Part family, part school, part living around Boston and seeing inequality close up. My friend group also talks about these issues a lot.

follow_ups.question: What issue feels most personal?
follow_ups.response: Housing affordability. Even with family help, rent feels absurd, and I know people making choices around that constantly.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have gotten more practical about politics. When I was younger, I thought having the right opinion online was almost the same as doing something. Recently I have cared more about actual local policy: zoning, transit, arts funding, public spaces, and who can afford to stay in the city. I am still progressive, but I am more interested in implementation now.

follow_ups.question: What caused that shift?
follow_ups.response: Living with rent pressure and seeing how city decisions affect everyday life.

follow_ups.question: Has social media shaped your politics?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but I try not to let TikTok or Instagram be the whole picture.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It has affected me somewhat to a lot, especially because I am white and grew up pretty protected from certain experiences. Black Lives Matter made me think more seriously about policing, who gets treated as suspicious, and what public safety should actually mean. It also made me notice whose voices are missing in tech and art spaces. I would not pretend I am directly affected the same way Black friends are, but it changed how I listen and what I pay attention to.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk about it with friends?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially during protests and after major news events.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect your creative work?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat. I became more careful about public-space projects and who they are for.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the issues are real and structural, not just individual bad behavior. Policing, housing, schools, and wealth are all connected. I also think people my age can be good at saying the right thing online but less good at staying involved when it gets boring or complicated. I am trying to learn more about local organizations instead of only reacting when something goes viral.

follow_ups.question: What local issues connect to that for you?
follow_ups.response: Police accountability, school funding, housing displacement, and public transit access.

follow_ups.question: Where do you learn about it?
follow_ups.response: Friends, local news, community groups on Instagram, podcasts, and sometimes city council clips.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race is built into so many systems that people want to call neutral. In tech, people talk about merit, but access to early computers, mentors, unpaid internships, and networks is not equal. In Boston specifically, there is this reputation for being educated and progressive, but the racial history and segregation are very real. I am still figuring out how to be useful without making it about myself.

follow_ups.question: Does your family talk about race?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, though not as naturally as my friend group does. I have had a few awkward but useful conversations with my parents.

follow_ups.question: Has your school environment shaped this?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Diverse classes and friend groups made it harder to ignore how different people's experiences are.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with friends and family, shared resources sometimes, and gone to a couple local demonstrations. I am not an organizer, but I try to show up when I can and be thoughtful.

follow_ups.question: What did you do at demonstrations?
follow_ups.response: Mostly marched, listened, and stayed with friends.

follow_ups.question: Do you post about it online?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but I try not to make performative posts just to look good.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My close friends are mostly left-leaning, so they take it seriously. Some have been more active than me, especially friends involved in campus organizations. My parents support the basic ideas but are more cautious about protest tactics and public safety language. We have had some debates, but nothing relationship-breaking.

follow_ups.question: Who is most active in your circle?
follow_ups.response: Maya has done the most organizing and mutual aid work.

follow_ups.question: What do disagreements with your parents sound like?
follow_ups.response: They worry about disorder or safety, and I push them to think about why people protest in the first place.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am healthy. I do not have a serious medical condition. My main issues are sleep, stress, and sometimes treating coffee like a food group. I play pickup basketball, jog the Charles sometimes, and walk a lot, so I am not inactive. But I am not disciplined in a gym-routine way, and late-night coding can mess with my sleep.

follow_ups.question: How many hours do you usually sleep?
follow_ups.response: Six to seven on average, worse during hackathons.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a primary care doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, through my family health plan.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Boston makes walking easy, and friends make basketball fun, so movement is not too hard. The hard part is routine. If I stay up until 2 a.m. working on a project, the next day falls apart and I eat whatever is nearby.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit comes easiest?
follow_ups.response: Walking everywhere.

follow_ups.question: What is the biggest obstacle?
follow_ups.response: Sleep consistency.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge. I sprained an ankle playing pickup basketball last year and had to stay off it for a couple weeks. I have had normal colds and stress headaches during finals or deadlines. No major diagnoses, broken bones, hospitalizations, or chronic conditions.

follow_ups.question: Did you get medical care for the ankle?
follow_ups.response: I went to urgent care because it swelled up, but it was just a sprain.

follow_ups.question: Does it still bother you?
follow_ups.response: Only a little if I overdo it, so I try to warm up now.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not seriously limited me. Sleep and stress can make me less productive, but I have not been unable to work or study because of health.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed commitments because of health?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a class or meeting when sick, but not often.

follow_ups.question: Any accommodations needed?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Nothing major in my immediate family right now. My grandparents have normal aging stuff, and that worries my parents sometimes, but I am not a caregiver. I have had friends struggle with anxiety and burnout, especially around school and job searches, and that has affected me emotionally.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with grandparents?
follow_ups.response: Not directly, mostly family visits and checking in.

follow_ups.question: How do you support friends?
follow_ups.response: Mostly listening, bringing food, or sitting with them while they finish work.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have been lucky because I am still on my parents' insurance. Getting appointments can be annoying, but I have not had to skip care because I could not pay. The biggest barrier is usually scheduling and remembering to do it. I know that is a privileged position compared to a lot of people.

follow_ups.question: Do copays affect decisions?
follow_ups.response: Not usually for me, though I do think about cost before urgent care.

follow_ups.question: Who manages insurance details?
follow_ups.response: Mostly my mom still, though I am trying to learn it.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Not really in a formal way. My family is pretty conventional about doctors. I drink ginger tea or use stretching videos when I feel run down, but I would not call that alternative medicine exactly.

follow_ups.question: Any supplements or herbal treatments?
follow_ups.response: Maybe vitamin D in winter, but nothing consistent.

follow_ups.question: Would you try acupuncture or similar care?
follow_ups.response: Maybe for pain or stress, but I have not done it.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I have had alcohol in social settings, but I am 18, so it is not a regular or legal bar-going thing for me. During stress I am more likely to overdo coffee, stay up late, and distract myself with music or code than drink.

follow_ups.question: How much coffee is typical?
follow_ups.response: Two cups on a normal day, maybe more during a deadline, which is not great.

follow_ups.question: Do friends drink around you?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes at parties, but it is not the center of my social life.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use prescriptions for coping, and I do not use pain meds except normal ibuprofen if I am sore. I have tried marijuana a couple times socially, but it is not something I rely on. The most recent time was months ago with friends watching a movie, and I honestly mostly got sleepy and ate chips.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about substance use?
follow_ups.response: Not for myself right now, but I try to be aware because stress culture can normalize bad habits.

follow_ups.question: What do you use instead when stressed?
follow_ups.response: Music, walking, calling a friend, or making something.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: My family pays through employer-based health insurance, and I am covered as a dependent. My own health expenses are low right now, mostly routine visits or urgent care once in a while. My parents handle most of the premiums and paperwork. I am aware that when I am older or employed, that will become more my responsibility.

follow_ups.question: Any medical debt?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Do you budget for health costs?
follow_ups.response: Not really beyond keeping a little savings for copays or emergencies.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am pro-vaccine. I got routine vaccines and COVID shots, and I see it as basic public health.

follow_ups.question: Any hesitation in your family?
follow_ups.response: Not much. My family is pretty mainstream on vaccines.

follow_ups.question: Do you get flu shots?
follow_ups.response: Usually, especially if it is easy at a pharmacy or clinic.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: I trust my doctor, CDC-type public health sources, and major hospital systems like Mass General Brigham. I also listen to science podcasts, but I try to check against actual medical sources. I do not trust random viral posts unless they link to something credible.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss vaccine info with friends?
follow_ups.response: Only casually. Most of my friends are vaccinated and not very conflicted about it.

follow_ups.question: Who in your family gives health advice?
follow_ups.response: My mom usually points me toward the doctor instead of guessing.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: The past year has been exciting but also kind of unstable emotionally. Finishing school, trying to figure out work, and comparing myself to people who already have jobs can mess with my head. I am usually optimistic and high-energy, but I get anxious when there is no structure. I have had stretches where I procrastinate, then panic, then overwork. Friends help a lot because they remind me I am not the only one in that weird transition.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I am working in creative technology or HCI, building things that people actually interact with in public spaces, museums, festivals, or city environments. I would like to have enough money to be independent, pay rent without stress, and travel a bit. Berlin's gallery scene is a dream trip, and Kyoto is on my list too. I also hope I still have friends around me and do not become someone who only works. Longer term, I could see doing a master's in Human-Computer Interaction and eventually starting a studio or small venture for immersive installations. I want my life to stay collaborative, experimental, and flexible, but with more stability than I have now.

follow_ups.question: What would success look like next year?
follow_ups.response: Having a paid role or internship, a stronger portfolio, and not relying so much on my parents.

follow_ups.question: What do you not want to lose?
follow_ups.response: My friends, curiosity, and the feeling that making weird things is allowed.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value creativity, friendship, independence, and learning. I like feeling that I can build something from a half-formed idea and share it with other people. I value family too, especially the safety net and grounding they give me. I also value openness, like being around people who are curious instead of judgmental. If I had to sum it up, I want a life where I am making things, learning constantly, and staying connected to people I care about.

follow_ups.question: What value guides your daily choices most?
follow_ups.response: Curiosity, though sometimes it pulls me away from practical stuff.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you those values?
follow_ups.response: My parents taught stability and education; my friends taught me to be bolder creatively.
